title: Can you structure these 8 investment case questions in two minutes each?
description: 8 investment case prompts to structure in two minutes each, with model answers, where to start and the trap to avoid.
hook: Yes: almost every investment prompt comes down to four questions. Is there a real need, do the economics pay back, what could go wrong, and is there a cheaper alternative, such as squeezing more out of what the client already has? Here are eight investment prompts, from battery plants to surgical robots: two minutes each, then open the model and compare.
body:
How to use this set

Give yourself two minutes per prompt. Build your structure around need, economics, risks and alternatives, but phrase each bucket in the client's terms. Then name the number that would decide the case: a cost per mile, a break-even volume, a payback period. The model shows the buckets, where to start and the trap. For the method, read how to decide on a big investment, and for the maths, payback and NPV worked examples.

1. Should a car maker build its own battery plant?

Show a model structure
  • Need: our battery demand and security of supply; supplier prices and lead times.
  • Make versus buy economics: cost per kWh of building against buying; payback and NPV.
  • Risks: fast-changing battery technology; our ability to run a plant at scale.
  • Alternatives: a joint venture or long-term supply contracts; buying a stake in a supplier.

Where to start: make versus buy cost per kWh over the life of the plant.

The trap: ignoring that battery technology may change before the plant pays back.

2. Should a supermarket open dark stores for 15-minute delivery?

Show a model structure
  • Demand: orders per dark store per day; density of customers within a 15-minute radius.
  • Economics per order: basket size and delivery fee; picking, rider and rent cost per order.
  • Cannibalisation: orders taken from our own stores and online service; net new profit.
  • Competition and operations: rivals' rapid-delivery offers; whether we can staff and stock it.

Where to start: economics per order. Rapid delivery tends to lose money per order until volumes are high.

The trap: assuming every order is new rather than taken from our own stores.

3. Should a UK university open a campus in Singapore?

Show a model structure
  • Demand: students in the region and what they will pay; competition from local and other foreign universities.
  • Economics: set-up cost, fees and staffing; break-even student numbers.
  • Quality and brand: teaching and degrees equal to the home campus; reputational risk.
  • Regulation and partners: local approvals; partner or go alone.

Where to start: demand. Will enough students pay close to UK-level fees to study in Singapore?

The trap: assuming demand at home carries over to a new market.

4. Should a delivery company switch its 2,000 vans to electric?

Show a model structure
  • Cost per mile: van price, energy and maintenance; resale value and grants.
  • Operations: range against daily routes; depot charging and charging time.
  • Investment and timing: upfront cost and financing; switch all now or as vans retire.
  • Other benefits and risks: clean-air zones and customer expectations; battery life and grid capacity at depots.

Where to start: total cost per mile over a van's life, not the purchase price. If an electric van costs $5,000 more up front, the fleet needs $10M of extra capital, which only makes sense if running-cost savings repay it within the van's life.

The trap: comparing purchase prices only.

5. Should a fashion retailer launch a loyalty programme?

Show a model structure
  • Customer behaviour: would members visit and spend more; share of sales from repeat customers.
  • Costs: rewards, app and marketing; rewards given to customers who would have bought anyway.
  • Data value: personalised offers; better buying and pricing decisions.
  • Competition: rivals' programmes; what makes ours different.

Where to start: rewards paid to customers who would buy anyway, the hidden cost of loyalty schemes.

The trap: counting all member spending as extra.

6. Should an online retailer build its own warehouse or keep using a third-party one?

Show a model structure
  • Cost per order: our cost at scale against the third party's fees; the volume needed to beat them.
  • Investment: building, automation and payback; flexibility if volumes change.
  • Service: delivery speed and errors; control over the customer experience.
  • Capability and risk: whether we can run a warehouse well; peak season.

Where to start: the volume at which our cost per order beats the third party's fee. See the outsourcing framework.

The trap: comparing costs at today's volume instead of planned volume.

7. Should a hospital buy a $2M surgical robot?

Show a model structure
  • Clinical benefit: outcomes and recovery times; which operations use it.
  • Economics: cost per operation including consumables; extra patients treated and shorter stays.
  • Capacity: surgeons trained and theatre time; operations per year needed.
  • Alternatives: sharing with another hospital; leasing instead of buying.

Where to start: operations per year needed. If each robotic operation saves $2,000 in shorter stays, the hospital needs 1,000 operations to recover the $2M, or 200 a year over five years, before consumables and maintenance.

The trap: buying for prestige without enough cases to use it.

8. Should a government back a new nuclear power station?

Show a model structure
  • Need: electricity demand and other low-carbon options; energy security.
  • Cost: build cost, overruns and cost per MWh; who pays, taxpayers or bill payers.
  • Risk: delays, safety and waste; financing over decades.
  • Alternatives: wind, solar with storage, gas with carbon capture; small modular reactors.

Where to start: cost per MWh against the alternatives, including the risk of overruns.

The trap: comparing build costs without allowing for delays.

How to score your answer: compare like with like

Take the battery plant. A common error is to compare the plant's upfront cost with one year of buying batteries. Compare cash flows over the same period instead.

Suppose building saves $60 per battery on 500,000 batteries a year: $30M of gross savings. The plant costs $400M and adds $10M a year of fixed running costs, so the net benefit is $20M a year. Simple payback is $400M ÷ $20M = 20 years, before discounting. That is a long time in a technology that changes quickly, so a joint venture or long-term contract may be the better answer.

Strong: "At $20M a year, the plant takes 20 years to pay back. Unless volumes double or supplier prices rise sharply, I'd lean towards a long-term supply contract and revisit in three years."

When you review your structure, name the one assumption that could reverse the answer: here, volume, battery chemistry or supplier pricing.
